newsitem.title: USA: Pittsburgh to seek state funds to boost region.
newsitem.headline: Pittsburgh to seek state funds to boost region.

text.p: A group of private sector leaders charged with making the Pittsburgh metropolitan region a tourist destination plans to seek state funds for five major development projects to boost tourism and create 100,000 new jobs in three years.

The cost of the projects -- including at least one new stadium and an expanded convention center -- could approach $1 billion, said Thomas Usher, chairman of the newly-formed Regional Renaissance Partnership.
Usher, also chairman of Pittsburgh-based USX Corp, said funding is not secured and added it will be "a significant challenge."

Usher announced the group's formation and purpose at a news conference on Thursday. It is comprised of officials from regional development groups as well as the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Pittsburgh Pirates.

Completion of the projects should create 100,000 new jobs by the year 2000 and boost tourism in the Pittsburgh region to 12 million visitors annually from a current level of 6 million annually, Usher said.

Job growth in the Pittsburgh metropolitan area has increased by 1 percent annually since 1993, a rate that lags behind the national average. The area also has lost tourism to surrounding cities including Cleveland, Baltimore, and Cincinnati.
Moreover, city officials have said a new baseball stadium is needed to keep the Pirates in Pittsburgh. The team currently has the lowest attendance in Major League Baseball.

The group was formed to complete five major development initiatives, all of which have been cited as crucial to the region's development by local government officials: expanding Pittsburgh's David L. Lawrence Convention Center and nearby hotel space; developing entertainment facilities in the city's cultural district and along its riverfronts; reconstruction or replacement of Three Rivers Stadium; constructing a new major league baseball park; and improving highways, transit systems and parking.

Three Rivers Stadium, which has been plagued with construction problems, generates about $1 million each year for the Steelers. City officials have said that improvements to the stadium could generate more money for the team.

"Each of (the projects) requires a major investment of public and private funds," Usher said. "They represent a significant financing challenge. But if we are to be a truly great region, we need to find a way to meet that challenge."
He said funding will likely come from federal, state, private and local sources but added: "What the mix of that will be, I can't tell you that. We don't know yet how it's going to be financed."
The state legislature is scheduled to begin considering legislation this spring concerning funding for regional economic development projects across the state.

"We must insure that our region receives its fair share of funding," Usher said. "We need to present a coherent plan to the governor and legislature in the next few months or we may lose the opportunity forever."

He said the plan will include details of the development projects and funding suggestions. He added that discussions about the projects and the need for funding have been held with federal, state and local representatives. "The reaction was very positive," he said.
Usher said the group has not yet determined what percentage of funding it will seek from the state and other sources.
